strengths: Novel framework effectively combining 3D Gaussian Splatting with physics-based particle simulation via Material Point Method, providing a technically sound solution to dynamic weather effect synthesis
Well-designed three-stage pipeline (Gaussian→Particle→Gaussian) with thoughtful bidirectional conversion that preserves original scene geometry while enabling realistic physics simulation
Effect-specific collision handling demonstrates careful attention to physically plausible behavior (e.g., snowflake accumulation on surfaces, rainfall wetting patterns)
Practical utility demonstrated across diverse weather phenomena (snow, rain, fog, sandstorms) with clear visual improvements over existing baselines in qualitative results
Fine-grained control over effect parameters (fog color, sand scale, snow particle quantity) enables flexible content creation, supported by visual demonstrations (Figure 4)
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective visual explanations, particularly Figure 2's pipeline overview
Includes ablation studies validating design choices (collision handling in Figure 7) and demonstrates versatility across multiple scenes
weaknesses: Primarily qualitative evaluation with limited quantitative metrics; Table 1 provides only CLIP Similarity and VQAScore for subset of effects, missing standard metrics (LPIPS, FID) and user studies for visual quality validation

Baseline comparisons are problematic: ClimateNeRF and GaussCurl solve different problems under different constraints; AutoVFX comparison acknowledged as unfair; no fair comparisons against simpler particle-based baselines

Moderate technical novelty as individual components (3D Gaussian Splatting, Material Point Method, particle systems) are well-established; Gaussian-particle conversion is relatively straightforward; main contribution is engineering the combination rather than algorithmic innovation

Limited experimental scope: only 4 public scenes tested; restricted to outdoor environments; no evaluation on challenging scenarios (heavy occlusion, complex geometry interactions, extreme weather conditions); no user-captured data

Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned; extensive manual parameter tuning required per effect (Appendix A.3); effect-specific appearance parameters lack clear generalization strategy; no analysis of parameter transfer to new scenes
Incomplete ablations: only collision handling studied; no ablations on appearance parameter generation or three-stage pipeline design; missing sensitivity analysis for key parameters
Simplified collision model based on surface projection may produce artifacts at mesh boundaries; limited validation of collision accuracy and unclear performance on complex geometries
Generalization limitations unclear: each effect requires carefully tuned parameters; applicability to new scene types, camera motions, or compound effects not demonstrated
Computational cost not thoroughly analyzed; 7 FPS mentioned but no detailed timing comparisons to baselines; scalability to higher resolutions unclear

Incomplete technical analysis: Equation (1) doesn't fully explain interaction between simultaneous effects; active particle tracking (Eq. 3) lacks validation; failure cases and error modes not systematically discussed

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem of adding temporal dynamics and weather effects to static 3D Gaussian scenes
Sensible hybrid approach combining 3D Gaussian Splatting with physics-based particle simulation via Material Point Method
Supports diverse effects (snowfall, rainfall, fog, sandstorms, object dynamics) within a unified framework
Visually compelling results demonstrating plausible weather accumulation and atmospheric effects
Comprehensive implementation details in appendix supporting reproducibility efforts
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (3DGS, MPM, collision handling) without significant methodological innovation; contribution is primarily engineering-level

Severely insufficient quantitative evaluation: Table 1 provides only 3 metrics on 2 effect types, with method underperforming baseline on F+S (0.36 vs 0.38 CLIP Sim); uses questionable metrics (CLIP similarity designed for semantic similarity, not physical plausibility)
Completely absent user studies: for perceptual quality of dynamic weather effects, subjective evaluation is critical yet entirely missing from evaluation

Unfair baseline comparisons: ClimateNeRF and GaussCtrl are not designed for this task; AutoVFX is acknowledged as unsuitable; no comparison to proper weather rendering or physics-based graphics baselines

Critical practical limitation: appearance parameters must be manually defined per-scene and per-effect (Section 3.4) with no automatic generation method, severely limiting applicability and generalizability
Computational efficiency inadequately addressed: 7 FPS mentioned only in appendix; no cost analysis vs. baselines, memory requirements, or bottleneck identification

Severely limited evaluation scope: all demonstrations on outdoor scenes with simple geometry; no evaluation on indoor scenes, complex geometry, or challenging scenarios; ~10-15 unique test scenes total
Shallow ablation study: only collision handling ablated (with/without); missing ablations on appearance parameter generation, MPM choices, and Gaussian-to-particle mapping decisions
Inconsistent quantitative performance across effects (CLIP Sim range 0.36-0.89) with no sensitivity analysis or failure case discussion
No evaluation of generalization across scenes or scene types; unclear how parameters transfer or how to predict them for new scenes

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: Integrating dynamic global weather effects into static 3D Gaussian scenes addresses a genuine gap in the literature between existing static editing and fully dynamic 4D generation.

Sound technical approach: The three-stage Gaussian-particle-Gaussian pipeline is elegant and well-justified, with appropriate use of Material Point Method for physically-plausible simulation and interaction handling.

Comprehensive framework demonstrating versatility: The method handles multiple weather types (snow, rain, fog, sandstorms) plus object dynamics (leaves, feathers, drones), showing breadth of applicability.
Convincing visual results: Qualitative results demonstrate realistic weather-scene interactions including proper occlusion, accumulation on surfaces, and physically-plausible density variations.
Strong reproducibility support: Comprehensive appendix with implementation details, GitHub references, specific parameters for each effect, and reported runtime (7 FPS).
Effective ablation studies: Figure 7 clearly demonstrates that specialized collision handling is critical—without it, dynamic effects fail to interact convincingly with geometry.
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective figures, particularly Figure 2 providing intuitive pipeline overview.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: ClimateNeRF and GaussCurl are static editing methods not designed for dynamic effects; comparisons feel somewhat like strawman arguments. Missing comparisons to other physics-based simulation or recent 4D Gaussian approaches.

Insufficient quantitative evaluation: Heavy reliance on qualitative assessment; CLIP Similarity and VQA scores are not specifically designed to measure weather effect quality. No ground truth comparisons to real video; missing standard metrics like PSNR/SSIM.
Absence of user study: No formal perceptual evaluation or assessment of whether effects are perceived as realistic by humans, leaving subjective quality claims unvalidated.
Unclear appearance parameter generation: Section 3.4 acknowledges parameters are manually selected or derived from text-to-3D without systematic approach. Practical bottleneck for adoption unclear.

Per-effect parameter tuning reduces scalability: Appendix A.2 reveals effect-specific physics parameters (snowfall Young's modulus 0.14 vs rainfall 0.08); generalization to novel effects or scenes uncertain.

Limited experimental scope: Only 6 main scenes, primarily from MipNeRF 360 and Tanks & Temples datasets; mostly outdoor well-lit scenes lacking geographic diversity, indoor environments, or extreme conditions.
Incomplete ablation studies: Only collision handling ablation shown; missing ablations on MPM necessity, mapping strategies, and Gaussian parameter effects. No parameter sensitivity analysis.
Acknowledged but unresolved limitations: Current approach doesn't handle camera motion, dynamic scene geometry, or complex scenes well (Section 4.4); scalability and robustness questions remain.
Generalization concerns: Method requires significant per-effect engineering with effect-specific collision techniques; extensibility to novel weather types or variations is unclear.
